paragraphs: Speech generators that produce audio one step at a time can sound convincing, but their many sequential operations make them awkward to run on hardware designed for parallel computation. This paper introduces a training method for highly parallel speech generators that does not require a formula for the probability of each generated waveform.

The method compares distributions of real and generated audio using a spectral energy distance. Its statistical guarantee concerns magnitude spectrograms, which describe how the strength of different frequencies changes over time. The distance is a proper scoring rule for that representation and can be estimated without bias from minibatches. Training with this objective does not require an adversarial opponent.

The authors report leading quality among implicit generative models under the cFDSD metric. They also combine their method with adversarial training and obtain higher human Mean Opinion Scores than GAN-TTS. These are distinct findings: the distance supports training on its own, while the reported human-evaluation improvement comes from the combined approach.
neurips-2020-a-spectral-energy-distance-.tldr: A spectral distribution-matching objective trains parallel speech generators without likelihood calculations and improves reported synthesis quality.

paragraphs: Learning physical motion involves more than matching observed changes: the resulting model may also need to respect laws governing energy and mass. Earlier neural approaches learned continuous-time equations that mimic energy conservation. This paper addresses the difficulty that practical computations advance through discrete time steps, where the desired energy behavior may no longer hold.

The proposed physical model builds a particular differential geometric structure into a deep energy-based formulation. Energy conservation or dissipation, along with mass conservation, follows from that structure. This makes the physical laws consequences of the model's mathematical construction rather than separate behaviors that it merely attempts to reproduce from observations.

The authors also introduce automatic discrete differentiation so that neural networks can use the discrete gradient method. This connects the structured model to computation at finite time steps while ensuring its energetic behavior in discrete time. The contribution therefore addresses both what physical relationships the learned model represents and how those relationships are maintained when the model is evaluated computationally.
neurips-2020-deep-energy-based-modeling-.tldr: A structured neural physics model and discrete differentiation algorithm preserve specified physical laws during discrete-time computation.

paragraphs: Differentiable architecture search makes discrete network designs accessible to gradient-based optimization by replacing them with continuous choices. The paper identifies a mismatch in common relaxations: optimizing those continuous choices need not correspond to optimizing the original architectures. This matters because the search ultimately needs to select a discrete network.

The authors use a variational graph autoencoder to map architectures injectively into a continuous latent space, meaning distinct architectures receive distinct representations. They present this space as an equivalent setting for optimization. A probabilistic exploration mechanism encourages the search to investigate alternatives, with the aim of avoiding locally attractive but inferior architecture choices.

A further component addresses catastrophic forgetting in the shared supernet used during search. The proposed architecture complementation method is intended to reduce forgetting that harms predictions and makes alternating optimization inefficient. The paper analyzes the approach and compares it experimentally with existing one-shot search methods. Its contribution combines a revised search representation, enhanced exploration, and an intervention on the shared model's training behavior.
neurips-2020-differentiable-neural-archi.tldr: The method searches an equivalent continuous architecture representation while adding exploration and reducing supernet forgetting.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent's abilities depend on the environments it encounters during training. Designing a useful collection by hand takes effort, while random variation may fail to create structure or track the agent's progress. Making environments maximally difficult can also produce tasks that cannot be solved.

The paper proposes Unsupervised Environment Design, in which developers leave environment parameters unspecified and a learning process chooses them. Its PAIRED method uses three participants: a protagonist learning to act, an adversary designing environments, and an antagonist allied with that adversary. The environment designer is rewarded for producing a gap between the agents' returns, using the antagonist's performance to expose challenges that the protagonist has not yet mastered.

This regret-based objective gives the designer a reason to create tasks that another agent can handle while the protagonist struggles. In the reported experiments, PAIRED generates a curriculum whose environments become increasingly complex. Agents trained this way also perform better when transferred directly to highly unfamiliar environments, connecting adaptive task generation with the measured transfer benefit.
neurips-2020-emergent-complexity-and-zer.tldr: PAIRED automatically generates increasingly complex training environments by rewarding performance gaps between two agents, improving reported zero-shot transfer.

paragraphs: With a limited labeling budget, a learner needs to discover which classes deserve attention. A knowledge base may list classes that barely occur in the data and omit classes that actually appear. The paper targets accurate classification of classes above a chosen frequency threshold while spending few annotations on classes below it.

The difficulty is that those frequencies are initially unknown and may be extremely uneven. The proposed active learning method uses contextual representations from language models to search explicitly for rare classes. It pairs that search with a statistical stopping rule: once a class is shown with high probability to fall below the target frequency, the algorithm stops devoting attention to it.

Searching for rare classes therefore helps determine when further annotation is unnecessary. The authors prove that their algorithm's cost is only a logarithmic factor above a hypothetical method given the true label frequencies. Experiments also show that automated search can substantially reduce the samples needed to reach target accuracy, supporting the value of combining targeted discovery with principled stopping.
neurips-2020-exemplar-guided-active-lear.tldr: Targeted class search and a statistical stopping rule help spend labeling budgets on sufficiently common classes.

paragraphs: Mean field games describe strategic interactions through an aggregate population rather than tracking every opponent separately. This paper studies continuous-time fictitious play as a learning process for such games with finitely many states. Its analysis covers finite-horizon and discounted settings and allows an additional source of noise shared across participants.

The central result concerns exploitability, a measure of how much an agent could gain by deviating from the current behavior. The authors prove that this quantity decreases at a rate of O(1/t) along the analyzed process. A decreasing opportunity to benefit from deviation provides a way to assess progress toward a Nash equilibrium, linking learning dynamics to a strategically meaningful error measure.

Numerical experiments support the theoretical analysis in both model-based and model-free settings. The paper also reports converging learning dynamics for mean field games with common noise, which it identifies as a first. Together, these contributions extend the settings covered by fictitious-play analysis and establish exploitability as a useful quantity for tracking convergence.
neurips-2020-fictitious-play-for-mean-fi.tldr: The paper proves O(1/t) exploitability decay for continuous-time fictitious play in analyzed mean field games, including settings with common noise.

paragraphs: A robot choosing how to grasp an object must consider both the gripper's position and its orientation. Many approaches first sample possible grasps using heuristics and then score them with a learned model. This creates a tension: sampling fewer candidates saves effort, but may overlook useful ways to grasp the object.

GPNet learns to propose a diverse collection of six-degree-of-freedom grasps directly from a single view of an unseen object, without knowing the camera view in advance. Its proposal module places grasp-center anchors at regularly spaced corners of a three-dimensional grid. This structure can support predictions that emphasize greater precision or greater diversity.

The authors introduce a synthetic grasp dataset and evaluate their method using rule-based criteria, simulation, and physical tests. They report advantages over existing methods and connect improved simulation results to the specified grasp coverage, which helps transfer to real testing. The stated contribution is thus both a learned proposal mechanism and evidence that its coverage of candidate grasps has practical value beyond scoring isolated predictions.
neurips-2020-grasp-proposal-networks-an-.tldr: GPNet uses structured three-dimensional anchors to predict diverse robotic grasps directly from a single unknown camera view.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks can create realistic images, yet some outputs fall outside the patterns represented by real data. Existing remedies may discard poor outputs after generation or restrict which latent inputs are used. The paper points out that these remedies leave training effort and model capacity invested in outputs that will ultimately be avoided.

Its proposed intervention happens before training: select which examples the generator will learn from. By changing the empirical training distribution through instance selection, the method directs the model toward high-density regions of the data. These are regions where training examples are more concentrated, making the composition of the dataset an explicit part of improving generation.

The authors report better sample fidelity, reduced model capacity requirements, and substantially shorter training time. The underlying argument links those outcomes to concentrating learning resources before the generator is built. This positions dataset selection as a practical control over what a GAN spends its capacity modeling, alongside methods that alter or filter the generator's outputs.
neurips-2020-instance-selection-for-gans.tldr: Selecting training instances before GAN training concentrates capacity on dense data regions and improves reported fidelity and efficiency.

paragraphs: Training reinforcement learning systems directly on physical equipment can be constrained by the difficulty of collecting enough experience. This paper tackles that problem for aligning a Mach-Zehnder interferometer, an optical instrument used in experiments. The agent receives camera images of interference fringes and learns to use that visual information for alignment.

Training takes place in a simulated environment. The agent is not supplied with hand-designed image features or prior information about the underlying physics. To prepare it for physical measurements, the simulation includes domain randomizations that represent measurement uncertainties. These variations expose the learner to differences it may encounter when moving from simulated images to the actual apparatus.

The trained agent is then transferred to a physical interferometer and successfully aligns it without additional fine-tuning. The authors report performance at the level of a human expert. The result demonstrates that, for this alignment task, simulation training with suitable uncertainty variation can produce a usable visual control policy without requiring a further learning stage on the real instrument.
neurips-2020-interferobot-aligning-an-op.tldr: An agent trained on randomized simulations aligns a physical interferometer from camera images without fine-tuning, reaching reported human-expert performance.

paragraphs: A robot demonstration shows what a person did, but may leave unclear which object properties or movement choices mattered. Imitation learning based only on motion and perception must infer that intent indirectly. This paper adds natural language as a channel through which an expert can explain important aspects of a demonstration.

During training, the system receives verbal descriptions alongside demonstrated actions. It learns relationships among the language, the visual scene, and the motion. The resulting visuomotor policy can then take new instructions at runtime, allowing a person to specify details such as the intended target and reduce ambiguity about how the learned behavior should be used.

The authors demonstrate the approach in simulation with a seven-degree-of-freedom robot arm and compare it with alternative methods. The contribution is the integration of unstructured language into learning from demonstrations and subsequent policy control. The reported setting supports the feasibility of language-conditioned manipulation policies, with language providing information that execution traces alone may leave unresolved.
neurips-2020-language-conditioned-imitat.tldr: Pairing demonstrations with natural-language descriptions teaches robot policies that can be directed more precisely through runtime instructions.

paragraphs: Neural networks build complex functions by composing simpler operations. Training these compositions with gradient descent can encounter gradients that become very small or very large, making learning-rate choices consequential. This paper investigates multiplicative weight updates as an optimization approach suited to that compositional structure.

The theoretical contribution is a descent lemma for multiplicative updates applied to compositional functions. Such a lemma provides a mathematical basis for relating an update to improvement in the objective. From it, the authors derive Madam, a multiplicative counterpart of Adam, and show that it can train state-of-the-art network architectures without learning-rate tuning.

The paper also adapts Madam to networks whose weights are represented in a logarithmic number system, enabling training with a natively compressed weight representation. This connects the optimizer's multiplicative form with how parameters are stored and updated. Finally, the authors discuss connections to findings about biological synapses. The work therefore links an optimization result, a practical training method, and a compatible approach to compressed neural networks.
neurips-2020-learning-compositional-func.tldr: A descent result for multiplicative updates leads to Madam, an optimizer demonstrated without learning-rate tuning and adaptable to compressed weights.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning builds a binary classifier from labeled positive examples and examples with unknown labels. A common assumption is that the labeled positives represent the positives the classifier will encounter. This paper addresses cases where that assumption fails, including shifts over time, changes between domains, and manipulation of the positive examples.

The authors show that even arbitrarily unrepresentative positive data can be used when unlabeled samples are available from both source and target distributions and the negative-class distribution remains fixed. That fixed-negative condition is central to the result. They develop two statistically consistent methods: one combines negative-unlabeled and unlabeled-unlabeled learning, while the other uses a recursive estimator of prediction risk.

Experiments span real-world datasets and different forms of positive bias, including cases where source and target positives occupy disjoint supports. The reported effectiveness shows how much positive-class mismatch the methods can accommodate under the stated setup. The paper also proposes a simplified general approach for addressing overfitting in PU risk estimation.
neurips-2020-learning-from-positive-and-.tldr: PU learning can tolerate arbitrary positive-class shift with source and target unlabeled data when the negative-class distribution stays fixed.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to separate different factors of variation in data. The symmetry-based framework gives this goal a precise form: transformations act through irreducible group representations on independent parts of the representation space. Which separation is appropriate depends on a decomposition of the symmetry group acting on the data.

The paper empirically finds that standard variational autoencoders do not generally develop these linear disentangled representations. Inducing them instead requires changing the loss landscape. The authors also show that representations with this mathematical structure are desirable under classical disentanglement metrics, connecting the symmetry-based definition with established ways of evaluating learned factors.

Their proposed method induces irreducible representations without requiring labeled action sequences, removing a requirement of earlier work. They investigate learning from action sequences whose intermediate states are unknown and robustness to visual noise. They also demonstrate learning four independent symmetries directly from pixels. These findings support a route to structured representations in which the transformations need not be supplied as labeled actions.
neurips-2020-linear-disentangled-represe.tldr: The paper induces symmetry-based linear disentangled representations without labeled actions and demonstrates learning four independent symmetries from pixels.

paragraphs: Low-dimensional node embeddings summarize networks using compact representations. A previous theoretical result suggested a serious obstacle: a particular low-dimensional model could not produce graphs that were both sparse and rich in triangles. Those properties matter because many real networks have relatively few edges overall but tightly connected local groups.

This paper shows that the obstacle depends strongly on the chosen model. A small relaxation permits sparse graphs with high triangle density, so the earlier impossibility result does not establish a general failure of low-dimensional representations. The authors further show that the relaxed model supports exact low-dimensional factorizations of many real-world networks.

They provide a simple algorithm based on logistic principal component analysis that finds such exact embeddings. Extensive experiments also demonstrate that very compact representations can capture local structure in real networks. The theoretical and empirical contributions reinforce the same point: assessing an embedding's expressive power requires examining the representation model, rather than attributing every limitation to low dimensionality itself.
neurips-2020-node-embeddings-and-exact-l.tldr: A small model relaxation enables low-dimensional embeddings to represent sparse, highly clustered networks and exactly factorize many real networks.

paragraphs: A hypernetwork generates the weights of another, primary network. This allows an output to represent an entire function, such as a network encoding shape or image information. The paper asks whether theoretical benefits associated with very wide conventional networks also apply when one network produces another network's parameters.

The authors show that making the hypernetwork infinitely wide does not by itself guarantee gradient descent will reach a global minimum. They then show that convexity can be obtained by enlarging its output to represent a wide primary multilayer perceptron. The distinction matters because width in the weight-producing network alone does not provide the same result as widening both networks.

For the regime where both widths become infinite, the paper derives Gaussian process and neural tangent kernels, naming the latter the hyperkernel. These characterize the architecture's functional priors and associated training description in that regime. The analysis also supplies tight bounds on higher-order Taylor terms for fully connected ReLU networks, contributing mathematical tools alongside the hypernetwork results.
neurips-2020-on-infinite-width-hypernetw.tldr: Infinite hypernetwork width alone does not guarantee global optimization, while widening both the hypernetwork and its generated network enables stronger theory.

paragraphs: Some systems change among discrete states while time runs continuously, and their true state is only partly observable. A decision maker must then estimate what is happening while choosing actions. This paper develops a mathematical description that brings those estimation and control problems together for finite state and action spaces.

Using optimal filtering theory, the authors formulate a continuous-time partially observable Markov decision process and derive a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman-type equation characterizing its optimal solution. This leads to a partial integro-differential equation, which they solve approximately with deep learning. The mathematical formulation supplies the target that the learned approximations seek to satisfy.

Two computational approaches are presented. One learns a value-function approximation offline; the other uses deep reinforcement learning online in belief space, where decisions depend on uncertainty about the hidden state. Demonstrations on toy examples establish applicability in those settings. The paper positions these results as groundwork for future methods addressing high-dimensional problems, rather than claiming that such problems have already been solved.
neurips-2020-pomdps-in-continuous-time-a.tldr: The paper formulates continuous-time POMDPs with finite states and actions and develops two deep-learning approaches to approximate their solutions.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks update node representations by collecting information from neighboring nodes. How that information is aggregated affects what graph patterns the network can distinguish. This paper extends expressiveness analysis beyond countable feature spaces to continuous features, which appear both in real inputs and in the internal representations of graph networks.

Within that extended framework, the authors demonstrate a requirement for multiple aggregation functions. They translate the result into Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation, an architecture that combines several aggregators with degree scalers. These scalers account for neighborhood size and generalize the role of summation, giving the network multiple ways to summarize the information surrounding each node.

The evaluation includes a new collection of tasks drawn from classical graph theory and existing benchmarks from real-world domains. The reported results demonstrate the model's strength across those evaluations. The contribution connects a theoretical issue about continuous features to an architectural choice, then tests whether that choice helps models capture and use graph structure in predictive tasks.
neurips-2020-principal-neighbourhood-agg.tldr: PNA combines multiple neighborhood aggregators and degree scalers, motivated by expressiveness requirements for graph networks with continuous features.

paragraphs: A few input-output examples often fit many possible programs, leaving a program synthesizer uncertain about what the user intended. A preference for simpler programs can resolve some ambiguity, but it does not use the fact that a person deliberately selected those examples. This paper treats that selection as part of a communication process.

The proposed approach evaluates a candidate program in two ways: whether it satisfies the supplied examples, and whether a rational person trying to communicate that program would have chosen those examples. Recursive reasoning about the speaker's intent therefore becomes an inductive bias. The examples provide evidence through both their contents and their suitability as a message.

The authors develop efficient algorithms for learning from input-output examples and implement a synthesizer in a simple grid-like layout domain. A user study finds that participants communicate more effectively with this pragmatic system than with a non-pragmatic counterpart. The result supports using a model of communication to interpret underspecified program requests in the studied domain.
neurips-2020-program-synthesis-with-prag.tldr: A program synthesizer resolves ambiguity by considering why a rational user would choose particular examples to communicate a program.

paragraphs: Image clusters discovered by a neural network may make sense to people even when they do not match an existing labeled dataset. That creates an evaluation problem: agreement with known categories cannot capture every understandable grouping. This paper introduces two measures intended to assess the interpretability of arbitrary visual groups, including automatically discovered ones.

Visual learnability measures whether people can infer a grouping from a small set of examples and apply it to new images. Describability asks whether a short textual description can replace those examples. Both turn interpretation into a task with observable classification behavior, instead of relying on an annotator's general impression that a cluster seems meaningful.

The authors also propose a captioning system that generates descriptions for entire visual classes to make the approach more scalable. They compare its descriptions with human descriptions using the describability measure. The framework separates two useful questions: whether a visual distinction can be learned from examples, and whether that distinction can be communicated concisely through language.
neurips-2020-quantifying-learnability-an.tldr: The paper measures visual-group interpretability through people's ability to learn groupings from examples or recognize them from concise descriptions.

paragraphs: Adding adversarial edges to a graph changes the information a node receives from its neighbors. The paper interprets these edges as contaminated samples entering a neighborhood aggregation function. With sums or means, even one extreme sample can distort the aggregate arbitrarily, and those distortions can accumulate through successive graph-network layers.

The authors introduce Soft Medoid, a fully differentiable generalization of the medoid motivated by robust statistics. Its breakdown point is 0.5: aggregation bias remains bounded when fewer than half of a node's edges are adversarial. This is a conditional guarantee about the aggregation operation, making the fraction of corrupted neighbors central to the result.

Because Soft Medoid is differentiable, it can be incorporated into end-to-end neural training. The authors report robustness improvements against structural perturbations by factors of three on Cora ML and 5.5 on Citeseer, with a factor of eight for low-degree nodes. These findings connect resistance to neighborhood contamination with improved empirical robustness of the resulting graph networks.
neurips-2020-reliable-graph-neural-netwo.tldr: Soft Medoid improves graph-network robustness using differentiable aggregation with bounded bias when fewer than half of a node's edges are adversarial.

paragraphs: Multicalibration provides a way to assess calibration across groups, making it relevant to group fairness. This paper separates the error in that fairness measure from ordinary prediction error. The distinction matters because choosing a trade-off between accuracy and fairness is a separate decision from determining how reliably either quantity has been measured.

The authors derive sample complexity bounds for uniform convergence of multicalibration error. These bounds specify how much data is sufficient to ensure that the error measured on samples is close to its population counterpart. The guarantee applies regardless of predictive accuracy, allowing confidence in the fairness estimate without tying it to a particular accuracy level.

The results cover both realizable and agnostic settings and do not depend on a specific algorithm category, such as differentially private methods. The authors also report improved sample complexity bounds over prior work. As a further consequence, their analysis yields uniform convergence guarantees for classical calibration error, extending the usefulness of the results beyond the multicalibration setting.
neurips-2020-sample-complexity-of-unifor.tldr: The paper bounds the samples needed to estimate multicalibration error reliably, independently of prediction accuracy and a specific learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Realistic generated faces are useful for supervision only if the relevant properties can be controlled accurately. For gaze-related tasks, this means changing eye direction and head orientation without confusing those changes with lighting, hue, or other appearance variation. The paper develops a face generator designed for this fine-grained control.

Its architecture learns to discover, separate, and encode additional appearance factors without requiring them all to be specified in advance. Explicitly separating these task-irrelevant variations improves the modeling of gaze and head angles. This makes the treatment of background appearance variation part of the solution to controlling the target properties.

Using a new evaluation scheme, the authors report improved redirection accuracy and better separation between gaze changes and head-orientation changes compared with the state of the art. They also show improvements in semi-supervised gaze estimation across datasets when real training data is limited. The findings connect more precise control of generated faces with a benefit for a downstream prediction task under that limited-data condition.
neurips-2020-self-learning-transformatio.tldr: Separating learned appearance factors improves control of generated gaze and head orientation and helps gaze estimation when real data is limited.

paragraphs: The paper begins with an observation: convolutional networks whose hidden responses better resemble primate primary visual cortex also show greater resistance to adversarial attacks. Motivated by that association, the authors build VOneNets, which place a fixed model of this early visual stage before a conventional neural-network back-end.

The front-end, called VOneBlock, combines biologically constrained Gabor filters, simple- and complex-cell nonlinearities, and simulated neuronal variability. These components implement a classical model of primary visual cortex. The design therefore makes a specific stage of visual processing more biologically faithful while retaining a back-end adapted from existing object-recognition networks.

After training, VOneNets retain high ImageNet performance and improve robustness on a combined benchmark of white-box attacks and common corruptions. The authors report improvements of 18% over base CNNs and 3% over state-of-the-art methods on that benchmark. They also find that the front-end's components act together to improve robustness, supporting the practical value of this particular biological modeling choice.
neurips-2020-simulating-a-primary-visual.tldr: Adding a fixed primary-visual-cortex model to CNNs improves reported robustness to attacks and corruptions while retaining high ImageNet performance.

paragraphs: Compressing high-dimensional data into a low-dimensional map inevitably changes some relationships among points. The useful question is which changes to discourage. When relevant class labels are available, they can help guide that choice, but separating classes too aggressively may damage the neighborhood structure that makes the map informative.

ClassNeRV introduces an objective that uses class annotations while accounting for two kinds of error: false neighbors, which appear close in the map despite being separated in the original data, and missed neighbors, whose original proximity is lost. It belongs to the theoretical family descending from Stochastic Neighbor Embedding and evaluates both neighborhood preservation and class-related distortions.

The authors report experiments in which ClassNeRV preserves neighborhood structure and class separation together, outperforming nine alternatives. This addresses a tension identified in earlier approaches: supervised maps often sacrifice neighborhoods for class separation, while unsupervised maps may preserve structure but mix classes. The result supports using labels to steer unavoidable distortion while still explicitly valuing local relationships.
neurips-2020-steering-distortions-to-pre.tldr: ClassNeRV uses class labels and neighborhood errors together to produce low-dimensional maps that preserve both local structure and class separation.

paragraphs: Video interpolation creates frames between recorded images, but the appearance of those images depends on exposure duration and the interval between frames. A method trained for one timing setup can misalign its predictions when a different camera uses different settings. This paper addresses interpolation when those temporal quantities are uncertain.

The authors derive a general curved-motion trajectory formula using either four consecutive sharp frames or two consecutive blurry frames, without requiring temporal priors. This provides a way to describe movement without fixing the input video's timing assumptions in advance. They also refine optical flow using constraints between neighboring motion trajectories to improve the interpolated results.

Experiments show that a single trained model can generate high-quality slow-motion video under the varied real-world conditions considered. The contribution connects a motion formulation that accommodates uncertain exposure and intervals with a refinement method that exploits relationships among trajectories. Its practical significance is that the reported model need not be restricted to one particular temporal prior when producing intermediate frames.
neurips-2020-video-frame-interpolation-w.tldr: A general motion formulation and optical-flow refinement enable frame interpolation without known exposure times or frame intervals.
